summary: This chapter from a psychology research methods textbook explains quasi-experimental research, which manipulates an independent variable without random assignment, placing it between correlational studies and true experiments in internal validity. It describes three designs: nonequivalent groups, pretest-posttest, and interrupted time series, and notes that combining a treatment and control group with pretests and posttests yields a stronger quasi-experiment. Threats such as history, maturation, regression to the mean, and spontaneous remission are discussed, including the Eysenck psychotherapy debate.
one_line: Explains quasi-experimental designs (nonequivalent groups, pretest-posttest, interrupted time series) and their threats to internal validity.
key_facts: Quasi-experimental research is research that resembles experimental research but is not true experimental research because participants are not randomly assigned to conditions or orders of conditions.
Quasi-experiments eliminate the directionality problem because the independent variable is manipulated before the dependent variable is measured.
Quasi-experiments do not eliminate the problem of confounding variables because participants are not randomly assigned.
A nonequivalent groups design is a between-subjects design in which participants have not been randomly assigned to conditions.
In a pretest-posttest design, the dependent variable is measured once before the treatment and once after it is implemented.
Regression to the mean is the statistical fact that an individual who scores extremely on a variable on one occasion will tend to score less extremely on the next occasion.
Spontaneous remission is the tendency for many medical and psychological problems to improve over time without any form of treatment.
Posternak and Miller found that participants in waitlist control conditions improved an average of 10 to 15% before they received any treatment at all.
Hans Eysenck's 1952 article summarized 24 studies showing that about two thirds of patients improved between the pretest and posttest.

By 1980, hundreds of randomized experiments on psychotherapy had been summarized by Mary Lee Smith, Gene Glass, and Thomas Miller, finding about 80% of treatment participants improved more than the average control participant.
An interrupted time-series design includes multiple pretest and posttest measurements of the dependent variable, with a treatment interrupting the series.
In a classic example, reducing factory work shifts from 10 hours to 8 hours was followed by a rapid and lasting increase in productivity.
Figure 7.3 illustrates a hypothetical study in which an instructor publicly taking attendance is the treatment and the dependent variable is student absences per week in a research methods course.
A combination design with treatment and control groups that both receive pretests and posttests is generally better than either the nonequivalent groups design or the pretest-posttest design alone.
If participants in a combination design are randomly assigned to conditions, the design becomes a true experiment rather than a quasi-experiment.
